How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Not very easy. There are plenty of good sites to find housing, but you have to start looking good time in advance because of the great demand for housing in Lisbon.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Housing is quite expensive both in Lisbon and at campus in Carcavelos. Expect to pay between €600-850 for a room/shared apartment. But I definitely recommend staying in Lisbon. The travel time is approx. 45-60 mins to campus, but to me it was definitely worth it to spend some time in the train when going to school in the weekdays and then be able to go "home" to Lisbon to stay in the evenings and weekends. Most events, places to go out etc. are located in Lisbon, and if you live close to school you have quite a trip home in the evenings/nights which - to me - was really nice to avoid. 
It's definitely a trade-off between long commutes to lectures in the weekdays if you live in Lisbon and long commutes to events and social gatherings in the evenings and weekends if you live close to school. Just be aware of this and consider it when you choose housing.

Also be aware of scammers when looking for housing. And read the reviews of the places (some apartments have issues with mold and/or cockroaches).

Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The bidding platform was difficult to navigate. Be aware that you need to be smart in regards to how you spend your bidding points on courses. Allocate few points to courses with many spots and/or few registered students, and allocate many points to the courses you really want and who has few spots/are in high demand.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You have a profile at a bidding platform. This platform has all the courses with descriptions, timetables, exam dates etc. And then it is up to you to make sure that you choose courses that do not overlap - both in terms of classes and exam times. 

After you have decided on courses, you use your bidding points to "bid" on each course. If there is great demand and few spots in a course, students will be allocated seats in accordance to how many points they have allocated relative to each other. So, as an exchange student it is difficult to know which courses are "popular" (and therefore would be wise to allocate many points to) and what courses you can get with few (or even zero) points. I would advice to look at the available spots as the main indicator for how many points to allocate. 

There are two bidding rounds. So, if you bid points on some courses in the first round and you do not get a spot in these courses, your points will be given back to you for you to use in the second round of bidding.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The International Mobility Office was very good a providing guides/online introductions and answering e-mails to assist with questions. But, as mentioned before, this was also necessary due to the pretty complex system you need to navigate in when your courses.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Spend a decent amount of time reading courses descriptions before bidding on courses. While this gives an idea of the content of each course, be aware that these descriptions are not always very good at describing the relative difficulty of the courses. As such local students will "try out" courses the first couple of weeks of the semester and change if they do not like the course. This option is not available to exchange students, and therefore you are "stuck" with the course you have been allocated to once the classes start. 

I took "Introduction to Machine Learning" as a course. The description of the course was relatively sparse, and once the classes started we observed many local students drop out as the teacher explained that this was an extremely demanding course with a high workload. However, as this point we as exchange students were fixed to the course. We spent many, many hours on this course, and it would have been nice if it had been stated in the course description how high the workload was, compared to other courses.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The courses varied greatly in difficulty. I think I have both had the easiest course and one of the most difficult courses (Introduction to Machine Learning --> NOT an introduction, if you ask me :))  ) of my university studies at NOVA on this exchange. In general, though, the courses are much easier than at UCPH.

The masters courses do also have a much smaller syllabus than we are used to at UCPH, since most of them are only 3,5 ECTS credits. As such, you should expect to have quite a lot of courses (I had 8 courses).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Smaller classrooms, maximum of 70 students. Closer relationship to your professor. They expect more classroom participation. Many more presentations in the classes. Grades are often a type of average between in-class presentations during the semester, hand-in's, and the final exam. The final exam typically weighs 50% of the final grade.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Economics of Health and Health Care
Environmental Policy
Economics of Health Systems
Financial Crises in History
International Migration
Impact Investments
Entrepreneurship
Introduction to Machine Learning

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Financial Crises in History was pretty fun. It was nice to learn about what happened in past financial crises, and to dive into the general characteristics/recurrent topics that they have in common. 

Economics of Health and Health Care was good as well. The professor was really nice, easily my favorite professor of this exchange.

International Migration was cool. The professor is pretty well-known for her contributions to this field of research and it was one of the most academic/research based courses I took.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Be ready to spend quite a lot of money on events and trips. In general it is quite cheap to travel, eat and sleep when going on trips, but it still took up the majority of my spending here. Travel costs are by far the greatest expense of the exchange, but Portugal has so many beautiful places to visit so I wouldn't hesitate to spend some savings here ;))

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Housing was more expensive than expected. Car rentals were way cheaper (!!). It was cheap to eat out at restaurants, but we did it relatively often so it was quite a big expense as well. Make sure to bring some savings in addition to the Erasmus grant and SU.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The Nova Student Union was very good at inviting us/including us in all of the events offered to local students. This was everything from parties, paintball games, sunset bars etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go travel!!! Porto, Nazaré, Peniche, Erriceira and many more places in the North. Lagos, Sagres and many more places in the South. You can also get very cheap tickets to Madeira or the Azores if you go out of season (maybe €40 for a plane ticket).

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Join the social events organized by the student union.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Not a problem. Very chill and open culture.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not any, really.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: They are very open to international students, workers, etc. Pretty quickly you don't feel like a visitor, but just as another international living and having their day-to-day life in Lisbon.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Allocate most of your money to housing, travels, and eating out. 

Housing was more expensive than expected, whilst travel and restaurants just offer so much more for your money compared to Denmark, so you have to make the most of this!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The courses have quite a lot of group work. This can be annoying since you spend quite a lot of time preparing presentations etc. with other students. Do not expect that you can just put in minimal effort, since you will often be placed in group work with local students and their grade will depend on your performance as well. So, even though the difficulty is not too bad, be prepared to spend some time at school anyway (because you have to sit with other students for group work).

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To experiencing the Portuguese culture and be given the opportunity to truly adapt and have your day-to-day life in these beautiful surroundings.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It was a bit annoying to spend so many hours studying and preparing presentations in groups. I expected to be able to go surf between lectures, and while that was possible sometimes, I often found myself with obligations to do some group work after or in-between lectures.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
